Common rounding procedures

Source: R/round.R
rounding-common.Rd

round_up() rounds ties upward, and round_down() rounds them downward. Otherwise, both agree with base::round().

They are special cases of round_up_from() and round_down_from(), which switch direction at a threshold other than 5.

Usage

round_up_from(x, digits = 0L, threshold, symmetric = FALSE)

round_down_from(x, digits = 0L, threshold, symmetric = FALSE)

round_up(x, digits = 0L, symmetric = FALSE)

round_down(x, digits = 0L, symmetric = FALSE)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The number to round.

digits

Integer. Number of decimal places to round to. Default is 0. Negative values round to powers of ten: round_up(1250, digits = -2) is 1300.

threshold

Numeric. Only in round_up_from() and round_down_from(). The point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step; greater than 0 and less than 10. round_up_from() rounds up when the part cut off is at least threshold tenths of a step, and round_down_from() rounds down when it is at most that many, so the two only differ for a value exactly on the threshold. round_up() and round_down() are the pair at 5.

symmetric

Logical. If TRUE, negative numbers are rounded like their absolute values. Default is FALSE. See Negative numbers.

Value

Numeric. x rounded to digits.

Details

These functions decide a tie by a fixed rule. base::round() rounds ties to even instead, and decides on the binary double rather than the printed decimal. They exist to reconstruct the output of software that rounds this way; see vignette("rounding-options") for which program uses which procedure. They are not meant to replace base::round() in original computations.

Negative numbers

By default (symmetric = FALSE), round_up() moves a tie to the higher number on the number line, so round_up(-2.5) is -2, and round_down(-2.5) is -3. This is what Stata does.

With symmetric = TRUE, a negative number is rounded like its absolute value, so a tie moves away from zero: round_up(-2.5, symmetric = TRUE) is -3. This is what Excel, SAS, SPSS, and Matlab do; IEEE 754 calls it roundTiesToAway.

For round_up() and round_down(), symmetric only affects ties among negative numbers. For round_up_from() and round_down_from() with a threshold other than 5, it affects every negative number whose cut-off part lies between threshold and 10 - threshold: round_up_from(-4.28, 1, threshold = 9) is -4.3, and -4.2 with symmetric = TRUE.

Under the package-wide default rounding = "up_or_down", both results are accepted, so symmetric cannot change a consistency verdict there.

Floating-point tolerance

Shifting a number by digits decimal places is not exact: 0.145 * 100 is stored as 14.499999999999998, just below the tie it is meant to be. All of these functions therefore nudge the shifted value by about 1.5e-9 before rounding, so that round_up(0.145, 2) is 0.15, as in the software being reconstructed. unround() reports bounds that assume the same tolerance.

The nudge is fixed, whereas representation error grows with x * 10^digits. Up to about 1e7 for that product, far beyond any reported summary statistic, the nudge dominates. Past it, a value exactly on a boundary may be rounded in either direction.

See also

round_ties_up() and friends are the same procedures under names that state the tie rule, so that symmetric need not be given. round_ceiling(), round_floor(), round_trunc(), and round_anti_trunc() always round in one direction.

Examples

# Except at a tie, all of these agree:
   round_up(x = 9.273, digits = 1)
#> [1] 9.3
 round_down(x = 9.273, digits = 1)
#> [1] 9.3
base::round(x = 9.273, digits = 1)
#> [1] 9.3

# At ties, they differ:
original <- c(
  0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45,
  0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95
)
tibble::tibble(
  original,
  round_up = round_up(x = original, digits = 1),
  round_down = round_down(x = original, digits = 1),
  base_round = base::round(x = original, digits = 1)
)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>    original round_up round_down base_round
#>       <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1     0.05      0.1        0          0  
#>  2     0.15      0.2        0.1        0.1
#>  3     0.25      0.3        0.2        0.2
#>  4     0.35      0.4        0.3        0.3
#>  5     0.45      0.5        0.4        0.4
#>  6     0.55      0.6        0.5        0.6
#>  7     0.65      0.7        0.6        0.7
#>  8     0.75      0.8        0.7        0.8
#>  9     0.85      0.9        0.8        0.8
#> 10     0.95      1          0.9        0.9

# Ties in negative numbers go up on the number line
# by default, and away from zero with `symmetric`:
round_up(x = -2.5)                     # Stata
#> [1] -2
round_up(x = -2.5, symmetric = TRUE)   # Excel, SAS, SPSS, Matlab
#> [1] -3

# A custom threshold moves the point at which
# rounding switches direction:
round_up_from(x = 4.28, digits = 1, threshold = 9)   # 8 < 9, so down
#> [1] 4.2
round_up_from(x = 4.28, digits = 1, threshold = 1)   # 8 >= 1, so up
#> [1] 4.3
